claim: In humans, DNA methylation marks inherited from gametes are largely erased following fertilisation, prior to construction of the embryonic methylome.
source: In humans, DNA methylation marks inherited from gametes are largely erased following fertilisation, prior to construction of the embryonic methylome.
evidence: This is a statement about established biological processes in human embryonic development, supported by scientific consensus.

claim: Rural Gambia experiences seasonal variation including changes in diet and nutritional status.
source: Exploiting a natural experiment of seasonal variation including changes in diet and nutritional status in rural Gambia
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work in this population.

claim: 259 CpGs show consistent associations between season of conception and DNA methylation.
source: we analysed three datasets covering two independent child cohorts and identified 259 CpGs showing consistent associations between season of conception (SoC) and DNA methylation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's analysis of three datasets.

claim: SoC effects on DNA methylation were most apparent in early infancy.
source: SoC effects were most apparent in early infancy, with evidence of attenuation by mid-childhood.
evidence: This is based on comparison of methylation data across different age groups in the study.

claim: SoC effects on DNA methylation show evidence of attenuation by mid-childhood.
source: SoC effects were most apparent in early infancy, with evidence of attenuation by mid-childhood.
evidence: This is based on longitudinal and cross-cohort analysis showing decreased effect sizes with age.

claim: SoC-associated CpGs are enriched for metastable epialleles.
source: SoC-associated CpGs were enriched for metastable epialleles, parent-of-origin-specific methylation and germline differentially methylated regions, supporting a periconceptional environmental influence.
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously identified metastable epialleles from published studies.

claim: SoC-associated CpGs are enriched for parent-of-origin-specific methylation.
source: SoC-associated CpGs were enriched for metastable epialleles, parent-of-origin-specific methylation and germline differentially methylated regions, supporting a periconceptional environmental influence.
evidence: This is based on comparison with PofOm loci identified in published studies.

claim: SoC-associated CpGs are enriched for germline differentially methylated regions.
source: SoC-associated CpGs were enriched for metastable epialleles, parent-of-origin-specific methylation and germline differentially methylated regions, supporting a periconceptional environmental influence.
evidence: This is based on comparison with gDMRs identified in published studies.

claim: The enrichment patterns support a periconceptional environmental influence on SoC-associated CpGs.
source: SoC-associated CpGs were enriched for metastable epialleles, parent-of-origin-specific methylation and germline differentially methylated regions, supporting a periconceptional environmental influence.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed enrichments and their known biological significance.

claim: Many SoC-associated CpGs overlap enhancers in H1 embryonic stem cells.
source: Many SoC-associated CpGs overlapped enhancers or sites of active transcription in H1 embryonic stem cells and fetal tissues.
evidence: This is based on analysis of chromatin state predictions from Roadmap Epigenomics data.

claim: Many SoC-associated CpGs overlap sites of active transcription in H1 embryonic stem cells and fetal tissues.
source: Many SoC-associated CpGs overlapped enhancers or sites of active transcription in H1 embryonic stem cells and fetal tissues.
evidence: This is based on analysis of chromatin state predictions from Roadmap Epigenomics data.

claim: Half of SoC-associated CpGs are influenced by measured genetic variants.
source: Half were influenced but not determined by measured genetic variants that were independent of SoC.
evidence: This is based on mQTL analysis in the EMPHASIS cohort.

claim: Genetic variants influencing SoC-associated CpGs are independent of season of conception.
source: Half were influenced but not determined by measured genetic variants that were independent of SoC.
evidence: This is based on testing mQTL for association with SoC and finding no significant associations.

claim: DNA methylation plays an important role in cell differentiation in mammals.
source: DNA methylation (DNAm) plays an important role in a diverse range of epigenetically regulated processes in mammals including cell differentiation, X-chromosome inactivation, genomic imprinting, and the silencing of transposable elements (TEs) (Smith and Meissner, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith and Meissner, 2013.

claim: DNA methylation plays an important role in X-chromosome inactivation in mammals.
source: DNA methylation (DNAm) plays an important role in a diverse range of epigenetically regulated processes in mammals including cell differentiation, X-chromosome inactivation, genomic imprinting, and the silencing of transposable elements (TEs) (Smith and Meissner, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith and Meissner, 2013.

claim: DNA methylation plays an important role in genomic imprinting in mammals.
source: DNA methylation (DNAm) plays an important role in a diverse range of epigenetically regulated processes in mammals including cell differentiation, X-chromosome inactivation, genomic imprinting, and the silencing of transposable elements (TEs) (Smith and Meissner, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith and Meissner, 2013.

claim: DNA methylation plays an important role in the silencing of transposable elements in mammals.
source: DNA methylation (DNAm) plays an important role in a diverse range of epigenetically regulated processes in mammals including cell differentiation, X-chromosome inactivation, genomic imprinting, and the silencing of transposable elements (TEs) (Smith and Meissner, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith and Meissner, 2013.

claim: DNA methylation can influence gene expression.
source: DNAm can influence gene expression and can in turn be influenced by molecular processes including differential action of methyltransferases and transcription factor (TF) binding (Jeltsch, 2006; Feldmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jeltsch, 2006 and Feldmann et al., 2013.

claim: DNA methylation can be influenced by differential action of methyltransferases.
source: DNAm can influence gene expression and can in turn be influenced by molecular processes including differential action of methyltransferases and transcription factor (TF) binding (Jeltsch, 2006; Feldmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jeltsch, 2006 and Feldmann et al., 2013.

claim: DNA methylation can be influenced by transcription factor binding.
source: DNAm can influence gene expression and can in turn be influenced by molecular processes including differential action of methyltransferases and transcription factor (TF) binding (Jeltsch, 2006; Feldmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jeltsch, 2006 and Feldmann et al., 2013.

claim: The human methylome is extensively remodelled in the very early embryo.
source: The human methylome is extensively remodelled in the very early embryo when parental gametic methylation marks are largely erased before acquisition of lineage and tissue-specific marks at implantation, gastrulation, and beyond (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2014.

claim: Parental gametic methylation marks are largely erased before acquisition of lineage and tissue-specific marks at implantation, gastrulation, and beyond.
source: The human methylome is extensively remodelled in the very early embryo when parental gametic methylation marks are largely erased before acquisition of lineage and tissue-specific marks at implantation, gastrulation, and beyond (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2014.

claim: The days following conception may offer a window of heightened sensitivity to external environmental influences.
source: The days following conception may therefore offer a window of heightened sensitivity to external environmental influences, potentially stretching back to the period before conception coinciding with late maturation of oocytes and spermatozoa at loci that (partially) evade early embryonic reprogramming (Fleming et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Fleming et al., 2018 and inference from the described reprogramming process.

claim: The window of environmental sensitivity potentially stretches back to the period before conception coinciding with late maturation of oocytes and spermatozoa.
source: The days following conception may therefore offer a window of heightened sensitivity to external environmental influences, potentially stretching back to the period before conception coinciding with late maturation of oocytes and spermatozoa at loci that (partially) evade early embryonic reprogramming (Fleming et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Fleming et al., 2018.

claim: Some loci partially evade early embryonic reprogramming.
source: The days following conception may therefore offer a window of heightened sensitivity to external environmental influences, potentially stretching back to the period before conception coinciding with late maturation of oocytes and spermatozoa at loci that (partially) evade early embryonic reprogramming (Fleming et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fleming et al., 2018.

claim: The effects of early exposures on the mammalian methylome have been widely studied in animal models.
source: The effects of early exposures on the mammalian methylome have been widely studied in animal models and periconceptional and early gestational factors including maternal folate and exposure to famine have been associated with DNAm changes in humans (Gonseth et al., 2015; Tobi et al., 2015; Finer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by the context and citations.

claim: Maternal folate has been associated with DNA methylation changes in humans.
source: The effects of early exposures on the mammalian methylome have been widely studied in animal models and periconceptional and early gestational factors including maternal folate and exposure to famine have been associated with DNAm changes in humans (Gonseth et al., 2015; Tobi et al., 2015; Finer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gonseth et al., 2015; Tobi et al., 2015; Finer et al., 2016.

claim: Exposure to famine has been associated with DNA methylation changes in humans.
source: The effects of early exposures on the mammalian methylome have been widely studied in animal models and periconceptional and early gestational factors including maternal folate and exposure to famine have been associated with DNAm changes in humans (Gonseth et al., 2015; Tobi et al., 2015; Finer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gonseth et al., 2015; Tobi et al., 2015; Finer et al., 2016.

claim: Causal pathways are difficult to elucidate in human observational studies.
source: However, causal pathways are difficult to elucidate in human observational studies, and even randomised experimental designs are prone to confounding due to reverse causation from exposure-related effects (Birney et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citation to Birney et al., 2016.

claim: Randomised experimental designs are prone to confounding due to reverse causation from exposure-related effects.
source: However, causal pathways are difficult to elucidate in human observational studies, and even randomised experimental designs are prone to confounding due to reverse causation from exposure-related effects (Birney et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Birney et al., 2016.

claim: Rural Gambia has repeating annual patterns of dry ('harvest') and rainy ('hungry') seasons.
source: Here, we address these limitations by exploiting a natural experiment in rural Gambia where conceptions occur against a background of repeating annual patterns of dry ('harvest') and rainy ('hungry') seasons with accompanying significant changes in energy balance, diet composition, nutrient status, and rates of infection (Moore et al., 1999; Dominguez-Salas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore et al., 1999 and Dominguez-Salas et al., 2013.

claim: Gambian seasons are accompanied by significant changes in energy balance.
source: Here, we address these limitations by exploiting a natural experiment in rural Gambia where conceptions occur against a background of repeating annual patterns of dry ('harvest') and rainy ('hungry') seasons with accompanying significant changes in energy balance, diet composition, nutrient status, and rates of infection (Moore et al., 1999; Dominguez-Salas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore et al., 1999 and Dominguez-Salas et al., 2013.

claim: Gambian seasons are accompanied by significant changes in diet composition.
source: Here, we address these limitations by exploiting a natural experiment in rural Gambia where conceptions occur against a background of repeating annual patterns of dry ('harvest') and rainy ('hungry') seasons with accompanying significant changes in energy balance, diet composition, nutrient status, and rates of infection (Moore et al., 1999; Dominguez-Salas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore et al., 1999 and Dominguez-Salas et al., 2013.

claim: Gambian seasons are accompanied by significant changes in nutrient status.
source: Here, we address these limitations by exploiting a natural experiment in rural Gambia where conceptions occur against a background of repeating annual patterns of dry ('harvest') and rainy ('hungry') seasons with accompanying significant changes in energy balance, diet composition, nutrient status, and rates of infection (Moore et al., 1999; Dominguez-Salas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore et al., 1999 and Dominguez-Salas et al., 2013.

claim: Gambian seasons are accompanied by significant changes in rates of infection.
source: Here, we address these limitations by exploiting a natural experiment in rural Gambia where conceptions occur against a background of repeating annual patterns of dry ('harvest') and rainy ('hungry') seasons with accompanying significant changes in energy balance, diet composition, nutrient status, and rates of infection (Moore et al., 1999; Dominguez-Salas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore et al., 1999 and Dominguez-Salas et al., 2013.

claim: The study assessed the influence of seasonality on DNA methylation in two Gambian child cohorts.
source: We assess the influence of seasonality on DNAm in two Gambian child cohorts (Moore et al., 2012; Chandak et al., 2017), one with longitudinal data, enabling robust identification of loci showing consistent effects at the ages of 2 years and in mid-childhood (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the study design and is supported by citations to the cohort descriptions.

claim: One cohort has longitudinal data enabling identification of loci showing consistent effects at 2 years and in mid-childhood.
source: We assess the influence of seasonality on DNAm in two Gambian child cohorts (Moore et al., 2012; Chandak et al., 2017), one with longitudinal data, enabling robust identification of loci showing consistent effects at the ages of 2 years and in mid-childhood (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: The study uses statistical models that make no prior assumptions about specific seasonal windows driving DNA methylation changes in offspring.
source: Through prospective study designs we capture conceptions throughout the year and, in contrast to previous analyses in this population (Waterland et al., 2010; Dominguez-Salas et al., 2014; Silver et al., 2015), we use statistical models that make no prior assumptions about specific seasonal windows driving DNAm changes in offspring.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach using Fourier regression.

claim: 768 SoC-associated CpGs show significant seasonal variation in 2 year olds from the ENID cohort with FDR < 5%.
source: We began by identifying 768 SoC-associated CpGs showing significant seasonal variation in 2 year olds from the ENID cohort with a false discovery rate (FDR) < 5% (Supplementary file 1a; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Fourier regression models revealed a heterogeneous distribution of year-round methylation peaks and nadirs at SoC-associated loci.
source: Fourier regression models revealed a heterogeneous distribution of year-round methylation peaks and nadirs at these loci (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on the Fourier regression analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SoC-associated loci are highly enriched for loci exhibiting SIV/ESS previously identified in multi-tissue screens in adult Caucasians.
source: SoC-associated loci were highly enriched for loci exhibiting SIV/ESS previously identified in multi-tissue screens in adult Caucasians (Kessler et al., 2018; Van Baak et al., 2018), hereafter named 'MEs' for short (Table 3; Figure 2B, 26 ME CpGs marked in red; enrichment p = 2.5 × 10–14).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published ME datasets and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All identified SoC-associated loci showed increased seasonal amplitudes compared to matched and random controls.
source: All identified loci showed increased seasonal amplitudes, defined as the distance between methylation peak and nadir, compared to matched and random controls (Supplementary file 1b; see Table 2 and Materials and methods for justification and further details on selection of controls).
evidence: This is based on comparison of seasonal amplitudes across different CpG sets.

claim: Loci with the largest amplitudes tended to show increased methylation in conceptions in the Gambian rainy season.
source: Loci with the largest amplitudes tended to show increased methylation in conceptions in the Gambian rainy season (Figure 2D left) in line with our previous observations in this population (Waterland et al., 2010; Dominguez-Salas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the relationship between amplitude and timing of methylation peaks, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: 61 loci were significantly associated with SoC (FDR < 5%) in the older EMPHASIS cohort.
source: Sixty-one loci (including three ME CpGs) were also significantly associated with SoC (FDR < 5%) in the older cohort (Figure 2D right).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the EMPHASIS cohort.

claim: The date of conception at methylation maximum was highly correlated across the two independent and different aged cohorts (Spearman rho = 0.7, p = 1.0 × 10–8).
source: Notably, the date of conception at methylation maximum was highly correlated across these two independent and different aged cohorts (Figure 2C left; Spearman rho = 0.7, p = 1.0 × 10–8).
evidence: This is based on statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No significant correlation was observed at matched controls with similar methylation distributions to SoC-associated loci.
source: No significant correlation was observed at matched controls with similar methylation distributions to SoC-associated loci (Figure 2C right).
evidence: This is based on statistical correlation analysis of control CpGs shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There were significant and relatively large effect size (SoC amplitude) decreases in the older cohort at the 768 SoC-associated loci.
source: Focussing on the 768 SoC-associated loci in the ENID cohort, we found significant and relatively large effect size (SoC amplitude) decreases in the older cohort, with SoC effect attenuation most marked at loci that are also putative MEs (4.1% median methylation decrease, Wilcoxon p = 2.8 × 10–6; non-ME CpGs: 1.9%, Wilcoxon p = 1.5 × 10–77; Figure 2E; Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is based on comparison of SoC amplitudes between cohorts, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SoC effect attenuation was most marked at loci that are also putative MEs (4.1% median methylation decrease, Wilcoxon p = 2.8 × 10–6).
source: Focussing on the 768 SoC-associated loci in the ENID cohort, we found significant and relatively large effect size (SoC amplitude) decreases in the older cohort, with SoC effect attenuation most marked at loci that are also putative MEs (4.1% median methylation decrease, Wilcoxon p = 2.8 × 10–6; non-ME CpGs: 1.9%, Wilcoxon p = 1.5 × 10–77; Figure 2E; Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of amplitude changes at ME vs non-ME CpGs.

claim: SoC amplitude changes in matched and random controls were much smaller (0.2%, p = 2.0 × 10–8).
source: Corresponding SoC amplitude changes in matched and random controls were much smaller (0.2%, p = 2.0 × 10–8).
evidence: This is based on comparison of amplitude changes in control CpGs.

claim: SoC effect estimates at SoC-CpGs were robust to different modelling strategies with respect to estimated blood cell composition and batch effects.
source: Sensitivity analysis confirmed that SoC effect estimates at SoC-CpGs were robust to different modelling strategies with respect to estimated blood cell composition and batch effects (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analyses described in the methods.

claim: A strongly consistent methylation signature was observed at n = 157 replicating SoC-CpGs in longitudinal ENID samples (Spearman rho = 0.7, p < 2.2 × 10–16).
source: This revealed a strongly consistent methylation signature at n = 157 replicating SoC-CpGs (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 1d; Spearman rho = 0.7, p < 2.2 × 10–16).
evidence: This is based on longitudinal analysis in the ENID cohort shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is further evidence of SoC effect attenuation with age at SoC-CpGs in longitudinal ENID samples (Wilcoxon signed rank test p = 6.7 × 10–12).
source: This analysis also provided further evidence of SoC effect attenuation with age at SoC-CpGs (Figure 3B; Supplementary file 1d; Wilcoxon signed rank test for difference in SoC amplitude p = 6.7 × 10–12 for SoC-CpGs and p = 1.0 for matched controls).
evidence: This is based on longitudinal analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The date of conception at methylation maximum at SoC-CpGs was highly consistent across all three datasets analysed.
source: Critically, the date of conception at methylation maximum at SoC-CpGs was highly consistent across all three datasets analysed, with a distinct pattern of methylation maxima for conceptions falling within the August-September period, most markedly at putative MEs with independent evidence of establishment in the early embryo (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on comparison across all three datasets shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a distinct pattern of methylation maxima for conceptions falling within the August-September period.
source: Critically, the date of conception at methylation maximum at SoC-CpGs was highly consistent across all three datasets analysed, with a distinct pattern of methylation maxima for conceptions falling within the August-September period, most markedly at putative MEs with independent evidence of establishment in the early embryo (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of timing of methylation peaks shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The August to September period corresponds to the peak of the Gambian rainy season.
source: The August to September period corresponds to the peak of the Gambian rainy season, a strong validation of our previous studies in babies and infants that focussed on conceptions at peak seasons only, with similar observations of higher methylation in conceptions at the peak of the Gambian rainy season compared to peak dry season (Waterland et al., 2010; Dominguez-Salas et al., 2014; Silver et al., 2015; Van Baak et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of Gambian seasonality and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Methylation minima fall within the February-April period, corresponding to the peak of the dry season.
source: Methylation minima fall within the February-April period, corresponding to the peak of the dry season (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: SoC-CpGs are distributed throughout the genome.
source: SoC-CpGs are distributed throughout the genome and cluster together in several regions (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is based on genomic location analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: SoC-CpGs cluster together in several regions.
source: SoC-CpGs are distributed throughout the genome and cluster together in several regions (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: 56 distinct SoC-CpG clusters and 105 'singletons' were identified using a maximum inter-CpG distance of 5 kbp.
source: Noting that the number of clusters is relatively insensitive to the inter-CpG distance used to define them (Appendix 1—figure 5), we identified 56 distinct SoC-CpG clusters and 105 'singletons' (SoC-CpGs with no close neighbours) using a maximum inter-CpG distance of 5 kbp (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis with specified distance threshold.

claim: 59% of SoC-CpGs fell within clusters using a 5 kbp distance definition.
source: With this definition, 59% of SoC-CpGs fell within clusters (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is based on the clustering analysis.

claim: SoC effect amplitudes were greater at SoC-CpGs falling within clusters than with singletons.
source: Of note, SoC effect amplitudes and cross-cohort correlations were greater at SoC-CpGs falling within clusters than with singletons (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This is based on comparison of clustered vs singleton CpGs shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: Cross-cohort correlations were greater at SoC-CpGs falling within clusters than with singletons.
source: Of note, SoC effect amplitudes and cross-cohort correlations were greater at SoC-CpGs falling within clusters than with singletons (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This is based on comparison of clustered vs singleton CpGs shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: A cluster mapping to IGF1R spans 872 bp and covers 7 CpGs.
source: Several SoC-CpG clusters extend over more than 500 bp, notably a cluster mapping to IGF1R which spans 872 bp and covers 7 CpGs (Supplementary file 1e, Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: This is based on analysis of cluster characteristics.

claim: All but one of the 7 IGF1R CpGs were significantly associated with SoC (FDR < 5%) in the older EMPHASIS cohort.
source: All but one of these 7 CpGs were also significantly associated with SoC (FDR < 5%) in the older EMPHASIS cohort (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the EMPHASIS cohort.

claim: SoC-CpGs are intermediately methylated compared to array background.
source: Compared to array background, SoC-CpGs are intermediately methylated, most notably at putative MEs (Figure 4B), and they tend to fall within CpG islands compared to array background and matched controls (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of methylation distributions shown in Figure 4B.

claim: SoC-CpGs tend to fall within CpG islands compared to array background and matched controls.
source: Compared to array background, SoC-CpGs are intermediately methylated, most notably at putative MEs (Figure 4B), and they tend to fall within CpG islands compared to array background and matched controls (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on genomic feature analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SoC-CpGs are highly enriched for MEs (21-fold enrichment, p = 3.0 × 10–23).
source: SoC-CpGs are also highly enriched for MEs (21-fold enrichment, p = 3.0 × 10–23, cluster-adjusted: 17-fold, p = 3.1 × 10–11; Supplementary file 1g; see Materials and methods for further details on cluster-based adjustments).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis comparing SoC-CpGs to known MEs.

claim: 24 SoC-CpGs directly overlap previously identified MEs.
source: The number of SoC-CpGs directly overlapping previously identified MEs is small (n = 24), although 49 SoC-CpGs (19%) fall within 100 bp of an ME (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis with known MEs.

claim: 49 SoC-CpGs (19%) fall within 100 bp of an ME.
source: The number of SoC-CpGs directly overlapping previously identified MEs is small (n = 24), although 49 SoC-CpGs (19%) fall within 100 bp of an ME (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is based on proximity analysis to known MEs.

claim: A large majority (n = 19/24) of overlapping MEs were identified in a previous screen for SIV.
source: Further investigation revealed that a large majority (n = 19/24) of overlapping MEs were identified in our previous screen for SIV, with a smaller number exhibiting ESS (n = 7/24; Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is based on comparison with different ME identification methods.

claim: No MEs overlap methylation distribution-matched controls.
source: No MEs overlap methylation distribution-matched controls.
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis with matched controls.

claim: Pairwise methylation states are highly correlated at a large majority of SoC-CpGs in both cohorts.
source: Pairwise methylation states are highly correlated at a large majority of SoC-CpGs in both cohorts, so that the same individuals tend to have relatively high or low methylation at multiple SoC-CpGs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Pairwise correlations at SoC-CpGs are not driven by increased correlation within SoC-CpG clusters.
source: Pairwise correlations are not driven by increased correlation within SoC-CpG clusters (Appendix 1—figure 8), and methylation at matched and random controls is uncorrelated, thus reducing the possibility that these correlations are driven by statistical artefacts.
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 8.

claim: Methylation at matched and random controls is uncorrelated.
source: Pairwise correlations are not driven by increased correlation within SoC-CpG clusters (Appendix 1—figure 8), and methylation at matched and random controls is uncorrelated, thus reducing the possibility that these correlations are driven by statistical artefacts.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of control CpGs.

claim: SoC-CpG reliability is classified as 'excellent' (median ICC = 0.76).
source: Finally, SoC-CpG reliability is classified as 'excellent' (median ICC = 0.76) using probe reliability estimates from a recent repeated measures study (Sugden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on comparison with reliability estimates from Sugden et al., 2020.

claim: Reliability of matched control CpGs is classified as 'good' (median ICC = 0.68).
source: Reliability of matched control CpGs is classified as 'good' (median ICC = 0.68) using the same method.
evidence: This is based on comparison with reliability estimates from Sugden et al., 2020.

claim: SoC-CpGs show a distinctive pattern of increased incidence of intermediate methylation states in post-gastrulation embryonic liver tissue.
source: As previously noted at putative MEs (Kessler et al., 2018), we found a distinctive pattern of increased incidence of intermediate methylation states at SoC-CpGs in post-gastrulation embryonic liver tissue, strongly contrasting with a general trend of genome-wide hyper- and hypomethylation at loci mapping to array background (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of embryo RRBS data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A similar pattern of increased incidence of intermediate methylation states was observed at distribution-matched controls in embryonic liver.
source: A similar pattern of increased incidence of intermediate methylation states was observed at distribution-matched controls.
evidence: This is based on analysis of embryo RRBS data for matched controls.

claim: There is a small but significant effect of increased methylation in rainy vs. dry conceptions at LINE1 elements (mean rainy season increase 0.02%, Wilcoxon p < 2.2 × 10–16).
source: This analysis confirmed a small but significant effect of increased methylation in rainy vs. dry conceptions at LINE1 and Alu elements (mean rainy season increase 0.02% and 0.01%, respectively, both Wilcoxon p < 2.2 × 10–16) suggesting a SoC effect on global methylation levels.
evidence: This is based on analysis of repetitive elements using REMP.

claim: There is a small but significant effect of increased methylation in rainy vs. dry conceptions at Alu elements (mean rainy season increase 0.01%, Wilcoxon p < 2.2 × 10–16).
source: This analysis confirmed a small but significant effect of increased methylation in rainy vs. dry conceptions at LINE1 and Alu elements (mean rainy season increase 0.02% and 0.01%, respectively, both Wilcoxon p < 2.2 × 10–16) suggesting a SoC effect on global methylation levels.
evidence: This is based on analysis of repetitive elements using REMP.

claim: SoC-CpGs tend to be hypomethylated in sperm compared to matched control CpGs and array background.
source: SoC-CpGs tended to be hypomethylated in sperm, compared to loci mapping to matched control CpGs and array background, respectively (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of sperm WGBS data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Intermediate methylation states at SoC-CpGs were preserved in both Gambian cohorts irrespective of sperm methylation states.
source: Intermediate methylation states at SoC-CpGs were preserved in both Gambian cohorts irrespective of sperm methylation states, in contrast to array background CpGs where methylation distributions strongly reflected sperm hypomethylation status (ENID cohort: Figure 4D left; EMPHASIS cohort: Appendix 1—figure 9 left).
evidence: This is based on comparison of methylation distributions stratified by sperm methylation status.

claim: SoC-CpGs show strong enrichment for PofOm CpGs (18-fold enrichment, p = 3.0 × 10–8).
source: We analysed 699 of these PofOm CpGs overlapping array background (Table 3) and observed strong enrichment for PofOm CpGs at SoC-CpGs and at all MEs on the array (18- and 15-fold enrichment, p = 3.0 × 10–8 and 1.8 × 10–36, respectively; Supplementary file 1h; Figure 5D right, PofOm CpGs marked as green triangles).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis with PofOm loci from Zink et al., 2018.

claim: All MEs on the array show strong enrichment for PofOm CpGs (15-fold enrichment, p = 1.8 × 10–36).
source: We analysed 699 of these PofOm CpGs overlapping array background (Table 3) and observed strong enrichment for PofOm CpGs at SoC-CpGs and at all MEs on the array (18- and 15-fold enrichment, p = 3.0 × 10–8 and 1.8 × 10–36, respectively; Supplementary file 1h; Figure 5D right, PofOm CpGs marked as green triangles).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis with PofOm loci from Zink et al., 2018.

claim: No enrichment for PofOm was observed at distribution-matched controls.
source: No enrichment was observed at distribution-matched controls (Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis of matched controls.

claim: PofOm enrichment at SoC-CpGs is driven by a large PofOm region spanning 6 CpGs on chr15 at IGF1R.
source: PofOm enrichment at SoC-CpGs is driven by a large PofOm region spanning 6 CpGs on chr15 at IGF1R (Supplementary file 1d); along with two singleton PofOm SoC-CpGs, one on chr18 close to PARD6G and the other in the Prader-Willi syndrome-associated imprinted region neighbouring MAGEL2, also on chr15.
evidence: This is based on analysis of which SoC-CpGs overlap PofOm loci.

claim: There is strong enrichment for oocyte gDMRs at SoC-CpGs (6.2-fold oo-gDMR enrichment, p = 2.3 × 10–16).
source: We next analysed SoC-CpGs and MEs and again found evidence for strong enrichment of oocyte, but not sperm gDMRs at these loci (6.2-fold oo-gDMR enrichment, p = 2.3 × 10–16 at SoC-CpGs; 2.9-fold, p = 1.2 × 10–24 at MEs), including after adjustment for CpG clustering (Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis with gDMRs from Sanchez-Delgado et al., 2016.

claim: There is strong enrichment for oocyte gDMRs at MEs (2.9-fold, p = 1.2 × 10–24).
source: We next analysed SoC-CpGs and MEs and again found evidence for strong enrichment of oocyte, but not sperm gDMRs at these loci (6.2-fold oo-gDMR enrichment, p = 2.3 × 10–16 at SoC-CpGs; 2.9-fold, p = 1.2 × 10–24 at MEs), including after adjustment for CpG clustering (Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis with gDMRs from Sanchez-Delgado et al., 2016.

claim: 14% (36/259) of SoC-CpGs overlapped oo-gDMRs.
source: Of note, 14% (36/259) of SoC-CpGs overlapped oo-gDMRs, in strong contrast to matched and random controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on overlap analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SoC-CpGs overlapping oo-gDMRs clustered into 19 distinct oo-gDMR regions.
source: These clustered into 19 distinct oo-gDMR regions (Supplementary file 1i) – more than six times the number identified as exhibiting PofOm by Zink et al. (three regions; Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of oo-gDMR overlaps.

claim: A large majority of SoC-CpGs that are hypomethylated in sperm are not oo-gDMRs.
source: A large majority of SoC-CpGs that are hypomethylated in sperm are not oo-gDMRs (i.e. they are not hypermethylated in oocytes) (Figure 5C and 5D bottom right), suggesting that factors associated with regional sperm hypomethylation rather than differential gametic methylation may be a key driver of sensitivity to periconceptional environment at these loci.
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Around half of all SoC-CpGs overlapped sites with predicted transcriptional or regulatory function in H1 ESCs and fetal tissues.
source: Around half of all SoC-CpGs overlapped sites with predicted transcriptional or regulatory function, with relatively few overlapping constitutive heterochromatic regions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on chromatin state analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Relatively few SoC-CpGs overlap constitutive heterochromatic regions.
source: Around half of all SoC-CpGs overlapped sites with predicted transcriptional or regulatory function, with relatively few overlapping constitutive heterochromatic regions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on chromatin state analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: SoC-CpGs are enriched for proximity to ERV1 endogenous retroviral elements.
source: Here, we found evidence that SoC-CpGs are enriched for proximity to ERV1 (Figure 7A top) but not ERVK retroviral elements (Appendix 1—figure 11; Table 3).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: SoC-CpGs are not enriched for proximity to ERVK retroviral elements.
source: Here, we found evidence that SoC-CpGs are enriched for proximity to ERV1 (Figure 7A top) but not ERVK retroviral elements (Appendix 1—figure 11; Table 3).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 11.

claim: SoC-CpGs show enrichment for proximal ZFP57 binding sites within 2 kbp.
source: Here, we found evidence for enrichment of proximal ZFP57 binding sites within 2 kbp of a SoC-CpG as previously observed at MEs, but we found no evidence for enrichment of proximal CTCF or TRIM28 binding sites in this array-based study (Figure 7A bottom; Appendix 1—figure 11; Table 3).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There is no evidence for enrichment of proximal CTCF binding sites at SoC-CpGs.
source: Here, we found evidence for enrichment of proximal ZFP57 binding sites within 2 kbp of a SoC-CpG as previously observed at MEs, but we found no evidence for enrichment of proximal CTCF or TRIM28 binding sites in this array-based study (Figure 7A bottom; Appendix 1—figure 11; Table 3).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 11.

claim: There is no evidence for enrichment of proximal TRIM28 binding sites at SoC-CpGs.
source: Here, we found evidence for enrichment of proximal ZFP57 binding sites within 2 kbp of a SoC-CpG as previously observed at MEs, but we found no evidence for enrichment of proximal CTCF or TRIM28 binding sites in this array-based study (Figure 7A bottom; Appendix 1—figure 11; Table 3).
evidence: This is based on enrichment analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 11.

claim: Half of SoC-CpGs had one or more associated mQTL.
source: Half of SoC-CpGs had one or more associated mQTL compared with 78% and 19% of matched and random controls, respectively; 92% of SoC-CpG mQTL were in cis (Table 4).
evidence: This is based on mQTL analysis in the EMPHASIS cohort.

claim: 92% of SoC-CpG mQTL were in cis.
source: Half of SoC-CpGs had one or more associated mQTL compared with 78% and 19% of matched and random controls, respectively; 92% of SoC-CpG mQTL were in cis (Table 4).
evidence: This is based on mQTL analysis in the EMPHASIS cohort.

claim: There was no difference in additional variance explained by significant mQTL between SoC-CpGs and both sets of control CpGs.
source: There was no difference in additional variance explained by significant mQTL between SoC-CpGs and both sets of control CpGs (Figure 7B; Table 4).
evidence: This is based on comparison of variance explained shown in Figure 7B.

claim: No significant SoC-mQTL associations were identified after accounting for multiple testing.
source: After accounting for multiple testing, no significant SoC-mQTL associations were identified (Supplementary file 1j and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on testing mQTL for association with SoC.

claim: SoC-methylation associations at SoC-CpGs are not confounded by genetic variation.
source: Our observations that (i) SoC-CpGs are distributed throughout the genome; (ii) SoC-CpG mQTL occur primarily in cis; and (iii) none are associated with SoC; strongly suggest that SoC-methylation associations at SoC-CpGs are not confounded by genetic variation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mQTL analysis results.

claim: No GxE (SoC) associations were identified after correcting for multiple testing.
source: Finally, we searched for GxE (SoC) effects, again performing separate tests for SNPs in cis and trans. No GxE associations were identified after correcting for multiple testing (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on gene-environment interaction analysis.

claim: Eighty percent of the population of the Kiang West region of The Gambia are of Mandinka ethnicity.
source: Eighty percent of the population of the Kiang West region of The Gambia from which the cohorts analysed in this study are drawn are of Mandinka ethnicity, with the majority of the remainder Fula (Hennig et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hennig et al., 2017.

claim: Results from ethnicity-adjusted sensitivity analysis were not materially different from those obtained for the main analysis.
source: Results from this ethnicity-adjusted sensitivity analysis were not materially different from those obtained for the main analysis (Appendix 1—figure 13; Supplementary file 1s).
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 13.

claim: None of the previously identified nutrition-related loci overlapped a SoC-CpG within 1 kbp.
source: However, a total of 57 previously identified loci did overlap or partially overlap array background. None of these overlapped a SoC-CpG within 1 kbp.
evidence: This is based on comparison with loci from James et al., 2018b review.

claim: A single CpG (cg17434309) mapping to IGF2 was within 1 kbp of two previously identified loci.
source: We also checked for overlaps with the larger set of SoC-associated CpGs not passing the 4% minimum effect size threshold, and found a single CpG (cg17434309) mapping to IGF2 that was within 1 kbp of two previously identified loci, one linking maternal plasma vitamin B12 with cord blood methylation (Ba et al., 2011), and the second linking gestational famine to blood methylation in older adults (Tobi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously published loci.

claim: 167 out of 259 SoC-CpGs have published associations in the EWAS Catalog.
source: This search produced published associations for 167 out of the 259 SoC-CpGs, mapping to 27 unique traits covering a range of pre- and postnatal exposures (Supplementary file 1l).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the EWAS Catalog.

claim: 109 SoC-CpGs have been associated with sex in previous studies.
source: Noteworthy amongst the most frequently reported associations with SoC-CpGs (Supplementary file 1m) in the context of our study were those with sex, gestational age, maternal smoking in pregnancy, maternal plasma folate levels, and adult body mass index (BMI) with 109, 45, 16, 6, and 1 associated SoC-CpG(s), respectively.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the EWAS Catalog.

claim: Multiple significant associations with infant sex were confirmed at SoC-CpGs in the ENID cohort.
source: We investigated some of these links using data from the 2 yr ENID cohort considered in our main analysis and confirmed multiple significant associations with infant sex but not gestational age or maternal folate at conception (Supplementary file 1n).
evidence: This is based on analysis in the ENID cohort.

claim: No significant associations were found between SoC-CpGs and gestational age in the ENID cohort.
source: We investigated some of these links using data from the 2 yr ENID cohort considered in our main analysis and confirmed multiple significant associations with infant sex but not gestational age or maternal folate at conception (Supplementary file 1n).
evidence: This is based on analysis in the ENID cohort.

claim: No significant associations were found between SoC-CpGs and maternal folate at conception in the ENID cohort.
source: We investigated some of these links using data from the 2 yr ENID cohort considered in our main analysis and confirmed multiple significant associations with infant sex but not gestational age or maternal folate at conception (Supplementary file 1n).
evidence: This is based on analysis in the ENID cohort.

claim: The observed SoC associations were not driven by confounding due to sex.
source: This, combined with our observation that sex is not associated with any tested batch or biological covariates (Supplementary file 1p-r), strongly suggests that the observed SoC associations were not driven by confounding due to sex.
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis and covariate analysis.

claim: Eleven SoC-CpGs mapped to SNPs associated with eight unique traits in the GWAS Catalog.
source: Eleven SoC-CpGs mapped to a total of 12 SNPs associated with eight unique traits in the GWAS Catalog (Supplementary file 1o).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the GWAS Catalog.

claim: Two SoC-CpGs are linked to childhood obesity traits in the GWAS Catalog.
source: Notable traits from a developmental programming perspective were those linked to childhood obesity (Comuzzie et al., 2012) (2 SoC-CpGs) and QRS traits associated with cardiovascular mortality in adults (1 SoC-CpG) (Evans et al., 2016; van der Harst et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the GWAS Catalog and supported by citations.

claim: One SoC-CpG is linked to QRS traits associated with cardiovascular mortality in adults in the GWAS Catalog.
source: Notable traits from a developmental programming perspective were those linked to childhood obesity (Comuzzie et al., 2012) (2 SoC-CpGs) and QRS traits associated with cardiovascular mortality in adults (1 SoC-CpG) (Evans et al., 2016; van der Harst et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the GWAS Catalog and supported by citations.
